title: Italian: Numbers, Days & Time
description: Count, tell the day and talk about today, tomorrow and yesterday. Plus why Italian weekdays are named after planets.

cards.details: Before a noun it becomes *un* or *una*: *un caffè*, *una birra*.
Pronounced DOO-eh, with two syllables. Handy for *due caffè* when you're not alone.
It sounds like English "tray", minus the glide at the end.
As in *pizza quattro formaggi*, the four-cheese pizza.
CHEEN-kweh. The *ci* is a "ch" sound, like in *ciao*.
Fun double duty: *sei* also means "you are" (*tu sei*). Context will tell you which!
Double consonants matter: hold the *tt* a beat longer, SET-teh.
Like the name Otto, and *otto e mezzo* (8½) is Fellini's famous film.
Close to Latin *novem*, which is also where English "November" comes from (it was the 9th Roman month).
dee-EH-chee. From 11 to 16 the numbers end in *-dici*: *undici, dodici, tredici…*
*Un(o) + dici* = one-and-ten.
From 17 up the pattern flips to ten-and-seven (*dici-a-sette*). In Italian folklore 17, not 13, is the unlucky number!
Also the plural of *vento* (wind), and the "venti" coffee size that a famous chain borrowed.
*Cinque* (5) + *-anta* (tens) = 50. The same pattern gives *sessanta* (60), *settanta* (70)…

cards.prompt: Spell out the number 100 in Italian.
cards.details: *Cento per cento* = 100%. Related to English "century" and "cent".

cards.prompt: Spell out the number 1,000 in Italian.
cards.details: The same *mille* as in *grazie mille* (a thousand thanks). Plural: *duemila* (2,000).
Also the name of the pasta course: the *primo piatto* (first dish).
The Moon's day (*luna*). Weekdays aren't capitalised in Italian, and that accent on the *ì* matters.
The day of Mars (*Marte*), the god of war.
The day of Mercury (*Mercurio*), the messenger god.
The day of Jupiter (*Giove*). English "Thursday" is Thor's day, another thunder god!
The day of Venus (*Venere*).
From "Sabbath". No planet here, and no accent either.
From Latin *dies dominica*, "the Lord's day".

cards.prompt: How do you say "today" in Italian?
cards.details: OD-jee. *Oggi è lunedì* = today is Monday.

cards.prompt: How do you say "tomorrow" in Italian?
cards.details: *A domani!* = see you tomorrow.

cards.prompt: How do you say "yesterday" in Italian?
cards.details: ee-EH-ree. Short, but easy to forget, so give it a second look.

cards.prompt: How do you ask "What time is it?" in Italian?
cards.details: Literally "what hours are they?". Plural, because it's usually more than one o'clock!

cards.prompt: How do you say "now" in Italian?
cards.details: *Ora* works too. Beware *subito* ("right away"), which in practice can mean anything up to "later".
From *sette* (seven), the seven days. *Fine settimana* = weekend.
